content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

12	
13	Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. 14	
15	The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.
16	
17	The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.
18	
19	Registration and retention by the lid
20	
21	The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.
22	
23	This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.
24	
25	The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.
26	
27	The circulation path
28	
29	In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.
30

Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.
32

34

A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.
36	
37	The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.
38

40	
41	The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. 44	
45	The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.
46	
47	The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. 48	
49	Operation

51	In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. In the following description, directional terms such as upper, lower, above, below, inward and outward refer to the carrier in its normal upright orientation with the insulated lid uppermost. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout the drawings.

Overall arrangement

Referring to FIG. 1, a passive cold-chain carrier 100 includes an insulated outer shell 10, a product tray 20 removably received in the outer shell 10, a thermal module 40 removably received in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and an insulated lid 60 closable on an upper edge of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 has a floor 12 and side walls 14 that rise from the floor 12 and bound an interior of the outer shell 10. The outer shell 10 and the insulated lid 60 are formed of thermally insulating material. The carrier 100 is reusable, the product tray 20 and the thermal module 40 being removable from the outer shell 10.

The product tray 20 is an upwardly open receptacle having a bottom wall and tray side walls 26, and receives the goods to be transported. A product region is the space within the product tray 20 that is occupied by those goods. Tray feet 22 depend from the product tray 20 and stand on the floor 12, so that the product tray 20 is supported above the floor 12 and a lower return passage 24 remains between the bottom wall of the product tray 20 and the floor 12.

The tray side walls 26 are spaced inward from the side walls 14 of the outer shell 10, so that two side supply passages 28 are formed, each side supply passage 28 extending downward between one tray side wall 26 and the confronting side wall 14. Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24. The tray side walls 26, one side supply passage 28 and the perforations 30 are seen in FIG. 4.

The thermal module

Referring to FIG. 2, the thermal module 40 includes a rigid spacer frame 42 and two opposed phase-change cassettes held by the spacer frame 42, namely a first phase-change cassette 44 and a second phase-change cassette 46. Each phase-change cassette holds a phase-change material, and the two cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42 in an upright, mutually facing arrangement so that an inner face of the first phase-change cassette 44 confronts an inner face of the second phase-change cassette 46 across a central space of the spacer frame 42. The phase-change cassettes are removable from the spacer frame 42, so that conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 before packing.

The spacer frame 42 rests above the product tray 20 and below the insulated lid 60. The spacer frame 42 defines a central inlet opening 48 that opens downward into the central space between the two phase-change cassettes, so that air rising from the product region enters the central space between the confronting inner faces. The spacer frame 42 further defines two downward guide ducts 50, seen in FIG. 4, each guide duct 50 located beside one of the phase-change cassettes, and peripheral outlet openings 54 positioned to align with the side supply passages 28.

The spacer frame 42 also defines a mating channel 56 that opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame 42, and carries resilient feet 58. The mating channel 56 and a rib entering it from above are shaped so that engagement between them during the closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally into position, rather than merely resting one upon the other.

Registration and retention by the lid

The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62 on an underside of the insulated lid 60, and a compressible lid gasket 64 carried on the underside of the insulated lid 60 and positioned to bear against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. The depending indexing rib 62, the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and the compressible lid gasket 64 are seen in FIG. 3. As the insulated lid 60 is closed, the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 of the spacer frame 42 and shifts the thermal module 40 into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28. The engagement is progressive: the depending indexing rib 62 first meets the mating channel 56 while the lid is still spaced above the outer shell 10, and the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62.

This sequence addresses the practical problem that the circulation path depends on an alignment which a person packing quickly at a bench cannot be relied upon to produce. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20, and the registration is completed by the closing of the lid. The alignment on which the circulation path depends is therefore created by an act the packer cannot omit, because a carrier that is not closed does not ship. The compressible lid gasket 64 bears against the upper edge of the outer shell 10 and is compressed only at the end of the closing travel, after the depending indexing rib 62 has completed registration, so that the carrier cannot be sealed shut around a thermal module 40 that is still out of position.

The same closing movement retains the thermal module 40. Ledges 18 of the outer shell 10 lie beneath the resilient feet 58 of the spacer frame 42, as seen in FIG. 3, and closure of the insulated lid 60 presses the resilient feet 58 against the ledges 18. The resilient feet 58 are compressed between the ledges 18 and the load path from the insulated lid 60, so that the thermal module 40 is held down and cannot lift away from the product tray 20 during transport. The resilient feet 58 maintain a downward holding force during transport, so the registered overlap between the peripheral outlet openings 54 and the side supply passages 28 that was established at closure persists through the journey.

The circulation path

In the registered position, the outer shell 10, the product tray 20, the thermal module 40 and the insulated lid 60 cooperate to define a circulation path. Air warmed by the goods rises from the product region within the product tray 20 and enters the central inlet opening 48. The rising stream divides along the faces of the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46, giving two cooling streams, and each cooled stream descends through one of the guide ducts 50 beside the phase-change cassettes, leaves the thermal module 40 through the peripheral outlet openings 54, and enters the side supply passage 28 registered beneath that peripheral outlet opening 54. Each descending stream then passes through the perforations 30 in the product tray 20 and returns through the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20.

The carrier 100 is free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover. Air warmed in the product region rises to the central inlet opening 48, and air cooled along the faces of the phase-change cassettes descends through the guide ducts 50 and the side supply passages 28, so that circulation proceeds without any powered air mover.

Condensate management

A condensate channel 70 is a shallow upwardly open trough extending around the product tray 20. A removable absorbent wick 72 lies in the condensate channel 70, and the condensate channel 70 and the absorbent wick 72 remain in the outer shell 10 when the product tray 20 is removed. Discharge openings 76 are provided at lower ends of the guide ducts 50 and discharge condensate into the condensate channel 70. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74 described below, one discharge opening 76 and the lower end of one guide duct 50 are seen in FIG. 5. Moist ambient air admitted whenever the carrier is opened condenses on the cold cassette surfaces and on the walls of the guide ducts 50, and the resulting water runs down the guide ducts 50 and is delivered through the discharge openings 76 to the condensate channel 70 rather than onto the goods.

The absorbent wick 72 carries a pull tab 74 that remains accessible when the product tray 20 is removed from the outer shell 10. A saturated wick is therefore drawn out and replaced as a service item between shipments, by lifting out the product tray 20 and pulling the pull tab 74, without opening a phase-change cassette and without taking the cassettes out of service to dry the interior.

Mechanical exposure indicator

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. FIG. 6 shows the mechanical exposure indicator 80 as it appears from outside the outer shell 10, at the outer surface of a side wall 14. Referring to FIG. 7, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 includes an indicator stem 82 movable between a stowed position and an exposed position, a temperature-responsive latch 84 that retains the indicator stem 82 in the stowed position, and a spring 86 biasing the indicator stem 82 toward the exposed position. The indicator stem 82 is thermally coupled to the first phase-change cassette 44. FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 show the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position.

The temperature-responsive latch 84 is arranged to release when the first phase-change cassette 44 softens. On release, the spring 86 moves the indicator stem 82 to the exposed position, in which the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10.

The exposed position is a latched position. The mechanical exposure indicator 80 retains the indicator stem 82 in the exposed position after the first phase-change cassette 44 has cooled again, and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is reset manually only after the carrier 100 is opened. A receiving inspection therefore sees the excursion even though the carrier presents itself as cold and the cassette as firm, and the record cannot be erased in transit by the cassette recovering. The indication is produced by the state of the refrigerant on which the payload depends rather than by a sensor at an arbitrary point in the air space, and requires no battery, no reading device and no data transfer.

The mechanical exposure indicator 80 does not control airflow. It neither opens, closes nor throttles the central inlet opening 48, the guide ducts 50, the peripheral outlet openings 54, the side supply passages 28, the perforations 30 or the lower return passage 24, and the circulation path is the same whether or not the mechanical exposure indicator 80 has moved to the exposed position. The behaviour of the carrier 100 is therefore unchanged by the act of reporting, and a tripped indicator does not degrade the protection given to the payload for the remainder of the journey.

Operation

In use, conditioned phase-change cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame 42 as the first phase-change cassette 44 and the second phase-change cassette 46. Goods are placed in the product tray 20 and the product tray 20 is placed in the outer shell 10 so that the tray feet 22 stand on the floor 12, leaving the lower return passage 24 beneath the product tray 20 and the two side supply passages 28 between the tray side walls 26 and the side walls 14. The thermal module 40 is placed in the outer shell 10 above the product tray 20. The insulated lid 60 is then closed, whereby the depending indexing rib 62 enters the mating channel 56 and shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position, the resilient feet 58 are pressed against the ledges 18 to retain the thermal module 40, and the compressible lid gasket 64 seals against the upper edge of the outer shell 10. Air thereafter circulates along the circulation path without operation of any powered air mover. At the destination, the insulated lid 60 is opened, the mechanical exposure indicator 80 is read and, if it stands in the exposed position, reset manually, the product tray 20 is lifted out with the goods, and the absorbent wick 72 is drawn out by the pull tab 74 and replaced if saturated.

Essential and optional features

Two phase-change cassettes are held by the spacer frame 42, opposed across the central space. Entry of the depending indexing rib 62 into the mating channel 56 during closing travel shifts the thermal module 40 into the registered position. The peripheral outlet openings 54 overlap the side supply passages 28 in the registered position. The condensate channel 70, the absorbent wick 72, the pull tab 74, the discharge openings 76 and the mechanical exposure indicator 80 are optional features, and a carrier 100 may be built with the registered circulation path and the lid-driven registration alone, or with any combination of the optional features.

The described implementations are examples. A person skilled in the art may combine, substitute or omit the described features within the scope of the claims that follow.

content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

content.text: I've read all inputs, all draft sections, the numeral table, and all seven figure briefs. Here is the completed source ledger and consistency review.

input.summary:
Ledger scope. The only inventor authority here is input/disclosure.md and the single USER message in input/conversation.md (identical text). The one other conversation turn is labelled "YOU" (the drafting agent reporting figure edits) and is therefore not support for anything it describes. input/brief.md was used only for title ("Passive Cold-Chain Carrier With Recirculating Side And Return Passages" — matches draft/01), no priority claim (draft/02 "Not applicable." — correct), and no federal sponsorship (draft/03 "Not applicable." — correct).

Traced clean. Every limitation of claims 1-20 traces to affirmative disclosure text: shell/floor/side walls/upper edge, tray on feet with lower return passage, tray walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, perforations, rigid spacer frame with two opposed cassettes, central inlet, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, mating channel, depending indexing rib shifting the module to the registered overlap, the full circulation path, absence of fan/pump/powered air mover, resilient feet pressed against ledges (cl. 2, 14, 18), gasket sealing after registration (cl. 3, 18), confronting inner faces across a central space with a downward-opening inlet (cl. 4), cassette removability (cl. 5, from "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"), condensate channel/wick/pull tab/discharge openings (cl. 6-8, 16, 19), and the mechanical exposure indicator with stem, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position, manual reset after opening, and no airflow control (cl. 9-11, 20). Claim 12 and the "progressive engagement" passage in draft/08 are supported by combining "the rib enters a mating channel ... and shifts the thermal module into a registered position" with "A compressible lid gasket seals against the upper edge of the shell after registration". The method claim 17 traces to the disclosure's use paragraph. Optional-feature framing in draft/08 §"Essential and optional features" matches the disclosure's own statement that the wick and indicator are optional and that the registered passive circulation path plus lid-driven registration is essential. Background prior-art framing is exempt from inventor support and contains no citations to trace. All 31 numerals in draft/numerals.md are used, each denotes exactly one part, and no numeral is used for two meanings. Section line 7-7 carries the same repeated designation in FIG. 6's brief, FIG. 7's brief, and draft/07 for both figures; the three broken-line curves in FIG. 1 are designated FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 consistently in FIG-1.md, in each enlarged view's brief, and in draft/07. Abstract is a single paragraph of ~141 words with no numerals and no scope beyond the claims. No drafting note, placeholder, open question or unresolved alternative remains in any draft/ file, and no application text uses "by way of example", "any closed outline" or similar renderer-justifying language.

Findings. Five issues, two critical.

1) Critical, untraced tray geometry. FIG-1, FIG-4 and FIG-5 verbalize a downward skirt on the tray side wall that continues below the bottom wall to a lower edge "spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough", and put the perforations in that skirt. The disclosure discloses only that the tray is "suspended above the shell floor by feet", that its side walls are "spaced inward from the shell side walls", and that air "passes through perforations in the product tray". There is no affirmative passage for a skirt below the bottom wall, for the elevation of its lower edge above the floor, or for its inboard/outboard position relative to the condensate channel. These are relative locations of a flow boundary and a port, so they are substantive even though FIG. 1 is called schematic; note also that the agent-authored "YOU" turn that introduced them is not inventor support.

2) Major internal-logic consequence of the same geometry: a lower edge spaced above the floor leaves an open route under the skirt, so air can reach the lower return passage without passing through the perforations. That contradicts draft/08 ("Perforations 30 ... open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24") and claims 1 and 17, which route the air through the perforations.

3) Critical, untraced rib/channel fit. FIG-3 states the groove's "width matches the thickness of the depending indexing rib 62 ... the two in contact", and draft/08 says the closing travel continues "until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62". The disclosure says only that "the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position". A dimensional width match, and seating of the channel on the rib, are fit and contact-topology assertions with no source, and a zero-clearance width also sits awkwardly with the same paragraph's requirement that the rib first meet a channel that is still out of position.

4) Major figure-to-figure inconsistency: FIG. 4 draws the bottom of the module body fragment (the tray wall is drawn below it, and the fragment is not said to be broken away) but gives the guide duct no opening at its lower end, while FIG. 1 gives every channel a downward opening at its lower end, FIG. 5 draws that opening as discharge opening 76, and draft/08 and claims 7 and 16 recite discharge openings at lower ends of the guide ducts (plural).

5) Minor terminology: FIG-4 and FIG-5 use bare "the fragment" for both the fragmentary view and the sectioned module body fragment in the same brief, leaving the module body's vertical extent ambiguous to a renderer.

Every finding below carries a filing-clean automatic fix confined to the figure briefs or to the identified sentence of draft/08; no fix adds a speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text.

Per the depiction-convention limit, exact relative locations, connections and flow-boundary geometry for a disclosed port remain substantive even where FIG. 1 is called schematic; a minimally specific opening through the tray at the junction of the two disclosed passages is all the source permits. The only text in the record describing this geometry outside the briefs is the drafting agent's own "YOU" turn in input/conversation.md, which is not inventor support.

findings.title: Untraced width-matched fit and seating contact between the depending indexing rib and the mating channel
findings.where: figures/FIG-3.md (paragraph beginning "To the right of the upright wall body"); draft/08-detailed-description.md (paragraph beginning "The insulated lid 60 carries a depending indexing rib 62")
findings.detail: The brief states a dimensional match between two parts (groove width equal to rib thickness) and asserts contact between them, and the description asserts an end-of-travel seating of the mating channel on the rib. The disclosure states only that the rib enters the mating channel and shifts the module into the registered position, and that the gasket seals after registration. A width-matched keyway fit and a seated load-bearing contact are exact proportion and contact-topology assertions about a functional joint, which remain substantive even where the geometry is schematic, and neither is anywhere in the source. The width match also sits awkwardly with the same paragraph's requirement that the rib meet a channel belonging to a module that is still out of position.
findings.evidence: FIG-3.md: "Its upper edge carries an upwardly open groove whose width matches the thickness of the depending indexing rib 62 and which receives the lower end of that rib, the two in contact." draft/08-detailed-description.md: "the remaining closing travel translates the spacer frame 42 horizontally until the mating channel 56 is seated on the depending indexing rib 62." Nearest source passage (input/disclosure.md): "As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages." The disclosure contains no statement about the width of the channel, the thickness of the rib, their relative dimensions, or any seating of one on the other.
